‘Make it Golden’

 

“The Burger Wars” aren’t going well for McDonald’s lately, and it has even bigger battles ahead.

 

Last week, Burger King owner Restaurant Brands International reported that comparable sales at the home of the Whopper jumped 8.4% from a year earlier. Some analysts predict McDonald’s will have a minus sign in front of the same measure when it unveils third-quarter results Wednesday. Its shares are trailing RBI’s by 25 percentage points in the past year.

 

The front lines ebb and flow, though. Investors shouldn’t overreact to short-term shifts because there’ll almost always be a juicier sandwich and a snappier marketing campaign to turn the tide.

 

Analysts and institutional investors are mostly focused on longer-term issues. These include the money being spent on renovations and equipment to remain competitive and how that creates tension with franchisees. Burger King is a few years into its “Reclaim the Flame” menu program and its “Royal Reset,” a carrot-and-stick approach to improving performance. They’re working.

 

McDonald’s recently announced its own initiatives, “Make it Golden” and “NEXT,” along the same lines. Within days of its late September investor day, when it outlined how much that would cost, its stock hit its lowest forward earnings multiple in more than a decade, aside from 2020’s Covid-19 panic.

 

The problem seems to be fears of middling bang for the buck and also how much the parent company must shell out to help franchisees. The outlay is coming at a time of strained finances for the chain’s core consumer. Meanwhile, materials and labor are expensive.

 

McDonald’s shares have presented a fantastic buying opportunity once a decade or so when investors wrongly concluded the company had lost its mojo. This isn’t one of those. McDonald’s has an impressive edge over competitors because of its strong digital-promotion game. The company says an incredible 220 million loyalty members are active worldwide on a 90-day rolling basis.

 

It’s more a matter of unfortunate timing—being asked to invest billions when that’s expensive and might pay off slowly. And that investment could produce a delayed effect on the bottom line. Analysts at Bank of America project that the greatest drag in terms of costs won’t come until 2030 or so.

 

The company recently pushed back its target of having 50,000 restaurants worldwide from next year into 2028. In the past year, analysts polled by FactSet have trimmed their 2026 through 2028 earnings per share expectations by 3.6%, 5% and 6.5%, respectively.

 

The stock price reflects a “show-me” attitude on the investments. It should work, but McDonald’s is no meal deal—the stock got cheaper for a reason.
